A_target.statement:
In [[Definition:Martin-Löf Type Theory|Martin-Löf type theory]], for $a, b, c : A$ there are terms:
:$\mathsf {sym} : a = b \to b = a, \quad \mathsf {trans} : a = b \to b = c \to a = c$
with $\map {\mathsf {sym} } {\mathsf {refl}_a} \equiv \mathsf {refl}_a$ and $\map {\mathsf {trans} } {\mathsf {refl}_a, q} \equiv q$.

B_source.statement:
Let $\map C {x, y, p}$ be a type family over $x, y : A$ and $p : x = y$, and $d : \prod_{x : A} \map C {x, x, \mathsf {refl}_x}$.
Then there is $J : \prod_{x, y : A} \prod_{p : x = y} \map C {x, y, p}$ with $\map J {x, x, \mathsf {refl}_x} \equiv \map d x$.
This is [[Definition:Path Induction|path induction]].

substitutions.the family C: y = x for symmetry, and the family of maps y = z -> x = z for transitivity

derived.the reflexivity case d: refl for symmetry, and the identity function for transitivity

object_map.reformulation: Reduce each property to its reflexivity case using the identity eliminator.

validity_conditions: The family for transitivity must quantify over the endpoint z, so that J is applied to a statement about all z.
The computation rule of J gives the stated judgmental equalities.
proof_plan:
For symmetry take $\map C {x, y, p} = \paren {y = x}$ and $\map d x = \mathsf {refl}_x$.
By the source result, $J$ gives $\mathsf {sym}$ with $\map {\mathsf {sym} } {\mathsf {refl}_a} \equiv \mathsf {refl}_a$.
For transitivity take $\map C {x, y, p} = \prod_{z : A} \paren {y = z \to x = z}$ and $\map d x = \lambda z. \lambda q. q$.

$J$ gives a term of this family, and $\map {\mathsf {trans} } {p, q}$ is obtained by applying it at $z = c$ to $q$.
By the computation rule, $\map {\mathsf {trans} } {\mathsf {refl}_a, q} \equiv q$.

Hence identity types carry the structure of an [[Definition:Equivalence Relation|equivalence relation]]; in homotopy type theory these are inversion and concatenation of paths.
{{qed}}
